To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the DNA binding specificity of analogs I and analog II is dependent on the extent of self-association.
the self-association properties and the binding specificity of N-propyl pyrrolecarboxamides are strongly dependent on the length of the peptide fragment.

analogs of netropsin containing two N-propyl-1-pyrrolecarboxamide groups linked covalently through a peptide chain exhibit a higher tendency to form intramolecular aggregates in aqueous solution than the analogs containing only one N-propyl-4-pyrrolecarbamide groups.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the synthesis of new DNA-binding ligands and with the study of the influence of the nature of the peptide fragment of these ligands on their ability to recognize and to discriminate among different DNA sequences.
the influence of the self-associative behavior of analogs I and 2 on their DNA binding properties.
the synthesis of a new class of netropsin-like ligands containing N-propylpyrolcarboxamide units.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the self-associated form of the netropsin-like ligand is responsible for the specificity of its binding to DNA.
the presence of self-associated species of the N-propylpyrolcarboxamide units in the netropsin analog affects the order of DNA base pair sequence recognition.
the binding of analog I and II to DNA is strongly influenced by their self-associated state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the binding specificity and binding affinity of the ligands are influenced by the conformation of the ligands in solution and by the presence of the trivaline peptide fragment.
the binding of N-propylyrrolecarboxamides and peptide fragments to DNA is dependent on the conformation adopted by the ligand in solution.
trivaline changes both the self-association properties of the N-propylpyrolcarboxamide units of analogs I and III and the binding properties of the peptide fragment of analog I with DNA.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the self-association of N-propyl pyrrolecarboxamides in solution is a prerequisite for their binding to DNA and that the binding of these ligands to DNA is dependent upon the extent of self-association.
the binding properties of the netropsin analog can be modulated by the introduction of a trivaline peptide chain.
self-associated species of netropsin-like ligands can recognize DNA sequences that are not accessible to monomers.
